paras: The threatened lynching of Anton Kloefel took place at Big Creek, near Weissport in Carbon County, Pennsylvania, on January 2, 1881, when a crowd called for hanging a New York bakery clerk who had just been arrested for shooting his wife. The constable lodged him safely in the Mauch Chunk jail, and within two weeks a jury acquitted him of manslaughter after evidence that the shooting was unintentional. The case drew notice because it followed a lynching in neighboring Northampton County, and a Lancaster paper used it as an argument against mob law.

Kloefel, a clerk in a Broadway bakery, had married Maria Bauchspiece about four months earlier, and the couple were spending the holidays at her father's farm at Big Creek in Franklin township. The Bethlehem dispatch placed the shooting just after the murder of the Geogles and the lynching of their killer, Snyder, which had caused great excitement in the Lehigh Valley.

On the evening of Sunday, January 2, his wife declined to sing "Pull for the Shore," and Kloefel took up a shotgun standing in the corner, capped it, aimed and fired, killing her with a shot through the left eye. Constable H. P. Levan arrested him on a warrant, and according to the Bethlehem dispatch, as Levan led him from the house there were cries of "Hang him" and "Serve him like the Northampton murderer!" The same dispatch said Kloefel asked for a revolver to "fix myself," offered no resistance, and was safely lodged in the Mauch Chunk jail.

Coroner C. W. Lentz's jury found that Maria Kloeffel died of a gunshot wound at her husband's hands, and a justice committed him for trial. By January 5 many people in the community believed the killing accidental, saying the gun had been loaded by her younger brother without Kloefel's knowledge. At the January term the grand jury indicted him for manslaughter and involuntary manslaughter, and on January 13 the jury acquitted him, although the judge had charged that it was "a clear case of involuntary manslaughter."

No arrest of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage. In August 1881 a Pennsylvania paper reported that Kloeffel had been jailed for a year for robbing a bank and that his old neighbors now thought he had killed his wife "in cold blood."

The story reached readers through a Bethlehem dispatch printed in the Delaware State Journal, the Alexandria Gazette, the Savannah Morning News, the Democratic Advocate and the Millheim Journal between January 6 and 13. Its headlines, such as "A Murderer's Coolness" and "A Young Wife Murdered," called Kloefel "the murderer" and reported the lynch cries without comment, while the Delaware paper headed it "A Narrow Escape from Lynching at the Hands of a Mob." The Lehighton Carbon Advocate, the local weekly, printed the fullest account of the shooting and inquest but said nothing of a crowd.

The Lancaster Intelligencer turned the case into an editorial, writing that the mob, "moved by the example of the Northampton people," had "well-nigh hanged an alleged wife-murderer" who proved not to be one, a lesson for those "advocating mob law and justifying lynch courts." The New York Sun reported the acquittal under the headline "The Slayer of his Bride Acquitted," and the paragraph was reprinted in New Jersey.

Reports differ on how close the crowd came to violence: the fullest dispatch describes only shouts, a Maine telegram summary said "a mob endeavored to hang him, but officers kept him safe," and the Lancaster editorial said he was "well-nigh hanged." The shooting itself was first reported as deliberate, with Kloefel quoted as saying "the devil entered my heart," but the trial evidence accepted by the jury was that he believed the gun unloaded.

bases: A crowd called for hanging an arrested man accused of killing his wife (A6, A11), and some reports said a mob tried to hang him (A4, A5); he was not harmed.

No one was killed: the accused was lodged safely in the Mauch Chunk jail (A6, A11) and later acquitted (A12, A13); the crowd's cries of 'Hang him' over an accused wife-murderer show a group acting under a pretext of justice (A6), but the episode stopped at a threat or at most an attempt (A4, A5).

The crowd's threat appears only in versions of one Bethlehem dispatch (A6, A7, A8, A11) and in summaries that rest on it (A4, A5); the local Lehighton weekly reported the arrest without any crowd or mob (A10).
